opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing the startup taught me is that ideals don't execute themselves. When I was in research, the ideal felt very clean. I wanted machine learning to be accessible, to run everywhere, on any hardware, and I believed if we built the right open-source abstractions, the world would naturally pick them up. Projects like XGBoost and TVM reinforced that belief a little, because the community really did grow around them.

When we started the company, I realized there's a whole other layer between a good idea and real impact. You have to figure out who actually needs this, what pain they feel today, and how to deliver something they can rely on, not just something that's elegant. That was humbling. Some things I thought were obviously important turned out to matter less to users than I expected, and things I considered "engineering details" turned out to be the entire product.

But I don't think it made me give up on the ideals. It made me more grounded about them. I learned to separate the long-term vision, which for me is still about making ML systems open and universally deployable, from the specific path to get there, which has to be flexible. You keep the north star fixed, but you're willing to change the route many times.

The other lesson is about people. In research you can push something forward almost alone if you're stubborn enough. In a company, and honestly in open source too, you only go as far as the team and the community you build. So pursuing an ideal became less about me being right and more about creating an environment where many people can contribute toward that shared goal.

Coming back to academia afterward, I think I bring that perspective with me. I still choose problems because I believe in them, but I also ask: if this works, how does it actually reach people? That question came directly from the startup years, and I'm grateful for it.

r001.rationale: The response says the specific path to the long-term vision has to be flexible and that you may change the route many times, conveying that the startup’s actual course can differ from what was originally expected.

r002.rationale: The response discusses adapting the path and building a team, but does not state that pursuing a startup requires reinventing oneself.

r003.rationale: The response says ideals need a practical route to real impact: understanding users’ needs and delivering something they can rely on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because for most of my career I never imagined I would be doing a startup. I was very much on the academic path. I did my PhD at Washington, built XGBoost and then TVM and MXNet, and I became a professor at CMU. I thought of myself as a researcher and a builder of open-source tools, and that felt like a complete identity.

What changed my view was realizing that the ideal I cared about, which is making machine learning accessible and efficient for everyone, on every device, could not actually be fulfilled from the research side alone. In academia, you can show that something is possible. You write the paper, you release the code, and you move on to the next problem. But "possible" is a long way from "usable." There's this enormous gap between a research prototype and something that a company can really depend on, that keeps working when the hardware changes, when the model architecture changes, when the user has a weird deployment constraint you never anticipated. Closing that gap takes sustained engineering effort, and you need an organization and real resources to do it. So with OctoML, and the work around TVM, the startup became the vehicle for actually carrying the ideal across that gap.

The second thing it taught me is that ideals have to meet reality, and reality is a very good teacher. When you're in research, you get to pick your problems. In a startup, customers pick your problems for you. Someone comes to you and says, my model takes two seconds per inference and I need it to be two hundred milliseconds on this particular chip, by next quarter. That's not the elegant problem you wanted to solve, but it tells you what actually matters. And very often it sends you back to the research with much better questions. Some of the most interesting technical directions I've pursued came out of that kind of friction, where the clean abstraction we designed just didn't survive contact with a real workload.

And the third thing, maybe the most important, is about people. I used to think of pursuing an ideal as mostly a personal matter, like it's my vision and I work hard toward it. The startup experience made me understand that the ideal only becomes real when a group of people choose to believe in it together, and when you build a structure where they can contribute. That's true for a company and it's also true for an open-source community. In some ways the two are the same lesson. You have to be humble about your own role. You set the direction, but a lot of the best ideas, and most of the actual work, come from others.

So I would say the startup didn't change my ideals. I still care about the same things I cared about as a graduate student: openness, efficiency, putting powerful models into the hands of people who don't have a thousand GPUs. What it changed is my understanding of what it costs to pursue them. It's slower than you expect, it requires compromises you didn't anticipate, and it depends on many more people than you. But I also came away more optimistic, because I've seen that when the engineering is done well, and the community is there, the ideal really does land in the world in a way that papers alone never achieve.

r001.rationale: He explains that startup customers set the problems, which can differ from the research problems he would have chosen, and says the startup became a vehicle for pursuing his ideal.

r002.rationale: He describes changing his view of startups and learning to work with others, but does not state that pursuing a startup requires reinventing oneself.

r003.rationale: He says the ideal could not be fulfilled through research alone and required sustained engineering, resources, and an organization to make it usable in practice.

astra-6.text:
I think the startup experience has made me more practical about how to pursue an ideal. It’s one thing to have a vision of what you want to build; it’s another to make something people can actually use and sustain the effort over time.

You have to listen to users, work with a team, and make choices under constraints. Sometimes that means changing your approach. I don’t think that necessarily means giving up on the ideal. It means being willing to learn how to get there.

So for me, the important distinction is between being persistent about the goal and being flexible about the path. You need conviction to keep going, but you also need enough openness to recognize when your original plan isn’t working.

r001.rationale: The response says the approach may change when the original plan is not working, but does not clearly state that what a founder ultimately does will differ from what they originally intended.

r002.rationale: It describes flexibility about the path, but does not state that pursuing a startup requires reinventing oneself.

r003.rationale: The response says startup experience made him more practical about pursuing an ideal, including building something people can use and sustain.

sol-6.1.text:
The startup experience has made me think about pursuing ideals in a much more concrete way. It’s easy to describe what you want to change; it’s harder to build something that actually helps people and can keep going over time.

You have to listen, work with other people, and be willing to change your approach. I don’t think that means giving up your ideals. It means distinguishing the thing you care about from the particular way you first imagined achieving it. You can stay committed to the purpose while being flexible about the path.

r001.rationale: The response says to be flexible about the path, but does not clearly state that what a founder ends up doing will differ from what they originally intended.

r002.rationale: It mentions changing one’s approach, but does not say that pursuing a startup requires reinventing oneself.

r003.rationale: The response says startup experience made pursuing ideals more concrete and describes building something practical that helps people and can continue over time.
